docs.title: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
docs.summary: A gait cycle is one stride of one leg: from the moment its heel strikes the ground to the moment the same heel strikes again. Inside that cycle the leg is either on the ground — stance — or moving through the air — swing.
docs.content:
Article: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
Section: 01 Two legs, one cycle
A gait cycle is one stride of one leg: from the moment its heel strikes the ground to the moment the same heel strikes again. Inside that cycle the leg is either on the ground — stance — or moving through the air — swing. In ordinary walking stance takes the larger share, and for a short period both feet are down at once.
One stride, drawn from GaitAI's own gait keyframes: heel strike, loading, mid-stance, toe-off, swing.
The other leg runs the same cycle, offset by roughly half a cycle. Symmetry is a comparison between the two: how alike are the left cycle and the right? That framing already contains the first surprise. The two cycles are drawn on the same clock, so they can differ in how long each phase lasts, in when each begins, and in how far the body travels during it — and those are three different comparisons.
keywords: what does gait symmetry actually mean?

docs.title: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
docs.sectionTitle: What a symmetry measure actually compares
docs.summary: The hero figure above lets you move each comparison on its own. Choose stance duration and one foot stays on the ground longer than the other. Choose swing duration and one leg spends longer in the air.
docs.content:
Article: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
Section: 02 What a symmetry measure actually compares (part 1 of 2)
The hero figure above lets you move each comparison on its own. Choose stance duration and one foot stays on the ground longer than the other. Choose swing duration and one leg spends longer in the air. Choose step timing and the right heel strikes early or late, so steps are no longer evenly spaced even if every phase has the same length.
Three families of symmetry, each answering a different question. Temporal — How long, and when: Stance time, swing time, double-support time — left against right; Step time: the interval between one heel strike and the next; Readable from a side view and from a wearable's timing signal Spatial — How far: Step length and stride length, left against right; Foot placement relative to the body's path; Sensitive to camera geometry, which the next story in Engineering GaitAI takes up
Because these are different comparisons, they can disagree. A person who protects one leg may spend less time on it — a temporal asymmetry — while keeping step lengths even. Another may take a shorter step with one leg at a normal rhythm. A single reported "symmetry" hides which of these happened, and the interpretation is different for each.
keywords: what does gait symmetry actually mean?
what a symmetry measure actually compares

docs.title: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
docs.sectionTitle: What a symmetry measure actually compares
docs.summary: Ratio, difference, index: Even within one comparison there are several ways to turn two durations into one number — a ratio, a difference, a normalised index. They behave differently at the extremes and they are not interchangeable.
docs.content:
Article: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
Section: 02 What a symmetry measure actually compares (part 2 of 2)
Ratio, difference, index: Even within one comparison there are several ways to turn two durations into one number — a ratio, a difference, a normalised index. They behave differently at the extremes and they are not interchangeable. A system should say which it uses; a reader should ask.

what a symmetry measure actually compares

docs.title: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
docs.summary: If the reference were a mirror, everyone would fail it. Healthy walking carries a small asymmetry — most people have a preferred leg for propulsion and another for support, the way they have a preferred hand — and that asymmetry is…
docs.content:
Article: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
Section: 03 Why nobody is perfectly symmetric
If the reference were a mirror, everyone would fail it. Healthy walking carries a small asymmetry — most people have a preferred leg for propulsion and another for support, the way they have a preferred hand — and that asymmetry is remarkably stable from day to day for the same person.
The informative reference is not symmetry. It is this person's own asymmetry, and whether it has moved.
This is the same argument the fourth Foundation makes for fall risk, arriving from a different direction. A symmetry value compared against a population cut-off tells you where a person sits among strangers. The same value compared against that person's own earlier walks tells you whether something changed — which is usually the question that was being asked.
A measure whose healthy value is "a little asymmetric, and stable" cannot be read as a pass/fail test. It has to be read as a trajectory, which means repeated measurement under comparable conditions — and conditions, it turns out, move the measure a great deal.
keywords: what does gait symmetry actually mean?

docs.title: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
docs.summary: A change in symmetry is a change in the comparison between two cycles. The person is one thing that can move it.
docs.content:
Article: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
Section: 04 What can make it move
A change in symmetry is a change in the comparison between two cycles. The person is one thing that can move it. Here are the others, and every one of them has produced a convincing asymmetry in a recording of someone who was walking exactly as they always do.
Things that change a symmetry reading without changing the person. Illustrative list; the size of each effect depends on the setup. 01 Surface: A slope, a kerb, a turn in the corridor. One leg does more work for a few strides. 02 Footwear: A stiff shoe, a heel, a slipper. Stance and push-off change on one side more than the other. 03 Carried load: A bag on one shoulder shifts the body's mass; the free side compensates. 04 Speed and fatigue: Faster walks are more symmetric for some people and less for others; tired walks drift. 05 Camera viewpoint: A camera off the walking axis foreshortens one side's step length. A spatial asymmetry that is in the geometry, not the gait. 06 Pose error: A misplaced ankle or a left/right swap inverts or invents an asymmetry for a span of frames — the previous story in AI Under Stress.
None of these is exotic. They are what a corridor, a care home or a sports hall looks like on a normal day. A system that reports symmetry without recording the conditions it was measured under is reporting a number it cannot interpret.
keywords: what does gait symmetry actually mean?

docs.title: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
docs.sectionTitle: Reading a change, not a number
docs.summary: Put the pieces together and a defensible reading of symmetry has four parts. Which comparison moved — stance, swing, timing, length — because they mean different things.
docs.content:
Article: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
Section: 05 Reading a change, not a number
Put the pieces together and a defensible reading of symmetry has four parts. Which comparison moved — stance, swing, timing, length — because they mean different things. How far it moved from this person's own baseline, because the population is the wrong reference. Whether the capture supports the comparison at all, because a foreshortened view or a filled-in joint can manufacture the whole effect. And whether it persists across walks, because a single asymmetric recording is one observation.
Which comparison → Against whose baseline → Under what capture → Across how many walks The four questions a symmetry reading has to answer before it means anything.
This is why, in a movement-intelligence system, symmetry does not arrive alone. It arrives with the cadence and stride variability of the same walk, the capture-quality judgement made before any number was computed, and the history it is being compared against. The signal is only as informative as the context that travels with it.
keywords: what does gait symmetry actually mean?
reading a change, not a number

docs.title: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
docs.sectionTitle: What symmetry can and cannot say
docs.summary: It can say that one side of a walk is behaving differently from the other, in a named way, compared with the same person's earlier walks.
docs.content:
Article: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
Section: 06 What symmetry can and cannot say
It can say that one side of a walk is behaving differently from the other, in a named way, compared with the same person's earlier walks. · It can say that the difference appeared after a change in conditions — or did not, which is the more interesting case. · It cannot say why. A protective pattern, a stiff shoe, a slope and a pose error can all produce the same number. · It cannot say that anything is wrong. It says that something is worth a closer look by someone qualified to take one.
That last line is not a disclaimer bolted on at the end; it is the design. A symmetry measure that knows what it compared, what it was compared against and how well it was captured is a good instrument. Read as a verdict, the same measure is a source of confident mistakes. The word decision support is the difference between the two.
keywords: what does gait symmetry actually mean?
what symmetry can and cannot say

docs.title: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
docs.summary: Symmetry is the most quoted movement measure because the idea is so clear: left should look like right.
docs.content:
Article: What Does Gait Symmetry Actually Mean?
Section: Closing
Symmetry is the most quoted movement measure because the idea is so clear: left should look like right. The measure earns its place when the idea is made precise — which comparison, whose baseline, what capture, how many walks — and loses it the moment a single number is asked to stand for all four.

docs.title: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
docs.summary: A camera does not record a walk; it records a projection of one. Which direction it flattens away decides which signals survive: a side view keeps the swing of the knee and loses the width of the stride, a front view does the reverse, and an oblique view keeps a little of everything while the scale changes under the person's feet. This is what that means for a system that has to measure movement from wherever the camera happens to be.
docs.content:
Article: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
Subtitle: The same walk, flattened eight different ways
Standfirst: A camera does not record a walk; it records a projection of one. Which direction it flattens away decides which signals survive: a side view keeps the swing of the knee and loses the width of the stride, a front view does the reverse, and an oblique view keeps a little of everything while the scale changes under the person's feet. This is what that means for a system that has to measure movement from wherever the camera happens to be.
Kind: Engineering Note
Category: Engineering GaitAI
Topics: Engineering · Movement intelligence · Research
Published: 2026-09-23
Author: GaitAI Research
Reading time: 9 minutes
The question it answers: Why does the same walk give a different answer from a different corner of the room?
Excerpt: A camera records a projection of a walk, not the walk. The angle decides which signals survive the flattening — knee flexion, stride width, timing, foot trajectory, body path — and a movement system has to be honest about which it has.
Opening: Put the same person on the same corridor and film them from the side, from the front, and from the corner where the building happens to have a camera. Three recordings of one walk — and a movement system will find three different sets of things it can measure well, measure badly, or not measure at all. · Nothing has changed about the walk. What changed is the direction the camera flattened it in. This is the most basic fact about video-based movement analysis and one of the least discussed, because in a research setting the camera is put where the measurement wants it. In a deployment it is put where the wall is. · The figures in this article are illustrative: a plan-view sketch of a walker and a camera, drawn to show which plane each angle sees. They are not a camera model, and the availability of each signal is stated in words — easier, harder, unavailable — never as a number.
What the reader takes away: What a side view sees that a front view cannot, and vice versa · Why oblique cameras are the common case and the hard one · How height, distance and lens quietly change the measurement
The two-minute version: A camera flattens three dimensions into two. Whatever moves along the line of sight is lost; whatever moves across it is kept. · A side view keeps the sagittal plane — knee flexion, stride length, the foot's arc, heel-strike timing — and cannot see stride width at all. · A front or rear view keeps the coronal plane — stride width, sway, foot placement — and foreshortens everything along the walk, hiding knee angles. · Oblique views, the common case for a mounted camera, see both planes partially, with a scale that changes as the person approaches or recedes. · Camera height, distance and lens decide how many pixels a limb gets, which bounds how precisely any joint can be placed. · A robust system declares what each view makes unavailable, favours features that survive the view it has, and never reports a measurement the geometry did not support.

docs.title: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
docs.summary: A body moves in three dimensions. An image has two. Every camera resolves that by discarding one direction — the one along its line of sight — and keeping the two across it.
docs.content:
Article: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
Section: 01 A camera is a projection
A body moves in three dimensions. An image has two. Every camera resolves that by discarding one direction — the one along its line of sight — and keeping the two across it. Movement along the line of sight does not vanish entirely; it appears as a change in apparent size. But a change in size is a much weaker signal than a change in position, and it is entangled with distance.
So the question for any camera is not "can it see the person" but "which plane of the person's movement is it looking across". Gait analysts name two planes: the sagittal plane, the side-on slice in which the legs swing forward and back, and the coronal plane, the front-on slice in which the body sways and the feet are placed left and right. A camera sees one of them well, the other badly, or both partially.
The camera does not choose what to measure. Its angle already has.

docs.title: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
docs.sectionTitle: What a side view gives, and what it cannot
docs.summary: Beside the walker, the camera looks across the sagittal plane. This is the textbook view, and for good reason: the knee's flexion and extension, the stride length, the arc the foot describes and the exact instant the heel meets the ground…
docs.content:
Article: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
Section: 02 What a side view gives, and what it cannot
Beside the walker, the camera looks across the sagittal plane. This is the textbook view, and for good reason: the knee's flexion and extension, the stride length, the arc the foot describes and the exact instant the heel meets the ground are all laid out across the image. Temporal measures read cleanly from here, because the events that define them — heel strike, toe-off — are unambiguous.
What the side view cannot see is anything that happens across the walk. Stride width — how far apart the feet are placed — is along its line of sight and collapses to nothing. Lateral sway is a small change in size. And the two legs overlap for part of every cycle, which is exactly the condition under which a pose estimator swaps left and right, as the first story in AI Under Stress showed.
Best for: Joint angles in the plane of walking, stride length, the timing of gait events, the shape of the foot's path. Weak or absent: stride width, sway, foot placement.

docs.sectionTitle: What a front or rear view gives
docs.summary: Turn the camera to face the walker and the picture inverts. Now the coronal plane is across the image: stride width, the side-to-side sway of the trunk, whether the feet land in line or splayed, whether one shoulder drops.
docs.content:
Article: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
Section: 03 What a front or rear view gives
Turn the camera to face the walker and the picture inverts. Now the coronal plane is across the image: stride width, the side-to-side sway of the trunk, whether the feet land in line or splayed, whether one shoulder drops. These are the signals that describe balance and support, and the side view could not give them.
The cost is everything along the walk. Stride length is foreshortened to a change in scale. Knee flexion — a rotation in the plane the camera is looking along — is nearly invisible. Heel strike is harder to place in time, because the event that marks it is a vertical motion seen at a shallow angle, and the person's apparent size grows every frame as they approach, so nothing can be compared frame to frame without correcting for it.
The two canonical views, and what each keeps. Side — Sagittal plane: Knee and hip angles; Stride length and foot arc; Heel strike and toe-off timing; Stride width: unavailable Front / rear — Coronal plane: Stride width and foot placement; Trunk sway and shoulder drop; Scale changes every frame; Knee flexion: unavailable

docs.title: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
docs.summary: Almost no deployed camera is a side view or a front view. Cameras are mounted high in corners, looking down and across a space, and the people in that space walk in whichever direction they were going.
docs.content:
Article: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
Section: 04 Oblique angles: the common case (part 1 of 2)
Almost no deployed camera is a side view or a front view. Cameras are mounted high in corners, looking down and across a space, and the people in that space walk in whichever direction they were going. The typical view is oblique: somewhere around forty-five degrees to the walk, from above.
An oblique view sees both planes — partially. Knee flexion is visible but compressed; stride width is visible but mixed with stride length; the foot's arc is a slanted ellipse. Every one of these can be recovered in principle, if the geometry is known. In practice the geometry is often not known precisely, and it changes as the person walks: a stride at the near end of the corridor covers many more pixels than the same stride at the far end.
What an oblique camera does to each signal, compared with the view that measures it best. Illustrative. 01 Knee flexion: Visible but compressed; recoverable only with a good estimate of the viewing angle. 02 Stride width: Mixed with stride length in the image; the two cannot be separated without the geometry. 03 Step timing: Available — the rhythm survives any view — but heel strike is placed less precisely. 04 Foot trajectory: A slanted, shrinking ellipse; its shape depends on where in the frame the foot is. 05 Body path: Actually improves: an elevated oblique view sees where a person goes in the room, which neither canonical view does well.

Section: 04 Oblique angles: the common case (part 2 of 2)
The oblique view is not a degraded side view; it is a different instrument with a different strength — spatial context — and a different weakness — every joint angle. A system designed for the side view and deployed on a corner camera will be confidently measuring things the image does not contain.

docs.title: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
docs.summary: Angle is the largest of the camera's choices but not the only one. Three quieter ones set the floor under everything a pose estimator can do. Height.
docs.content:
Article: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
Section: 05 Height, distance and lens
Angle is the largest of the camera's choices but not the only one. Three quieter ones set the floor under everything a pose estimator can do.
Height. A camera above head height looks down on the walker, so vertical motion — the foot lifting and landing — is seen at an angle and the ground plane is tilted in the image. Heel strike timing gets harder to place; body path gets easier to read. · Distance. Further away, the person occupies fewer pixels. A shin that is thirty pixels long can carry a knee that is right to within a pixel or two; a shin that is eight pixels long cannot. Precision is bounded by pixels per limb before any model is involved. · Lens. A wide lens covers the room and bends straight lines near its edges; a long lens sees a narrow slice with less distortion. The same walk at the edge of a wide frame is not the same shape as at its centre.
None of these are properties of the person and all of them change the measurement. A recording made from a different mount, or after a camera was moved by a few centimetres, is not directly comparable to the one before — which is why a longitudinal reading has to record its capture geometry alongside its values.

docs.sectionTitle: Designing for the angle you have
docs.summary: An engineering team cannot move the walls. What it can do is treat the view as a first-class input rather than a nuisance. Declare what is unavailable. If the geometry does not support knee flexion, do not compute it.
docs.content:
Article: Camera Angle Changes What AI Sees
Section: 06 Designing for the angle you have (part 1 of 2)
An engineering team cannot move the walls. What it can do is treat the view as a first-class input rather than a nuisance.
Declare what is unavailable. If the geometry does not support knee flexion, do not compute it. A withheld measure is honest; a foreshortened one is a wrong number with a confident label. · Prefer signals that survive the view. Rhythm, cadence and step-to-step variability are properties of timing, and timing survives almost any angle. Lean on them where the geometry is poor. · Estimate the geometry, and say how well. A known camera height and angle turns an oblique view back into measurements; an unknown one should lower the confidence of every spatial value, explicitly. · Use a second sensor for what the view cannot see. A wearable measures heel strike in the body's frame, not the camera's. The fifth Foundation's caution applies: fusion adds coverage only when the streams are honest about their own quality. · Compare like with like. Two recordings from different mounts are two instruments. A trend is only a trend if the capture geometry was the same, or was corrected for.

docs.title: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
docs.summary: Strip a walking video down: remove the face, keep only the silhouette, keep only the skeleton, keep only the paths the joints trace. Each step removes something that could identify a person and keeps something that still might. Where identity actually disappears is not a property of the picture; it depends on what is stored, what it is combined with, how long it persists and what it is for.
docs.content:
Article: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
Subtitle: There is no single point where a person disappears from the data
Standfirst: Strip a walking video down: remove the face, keep only the silhouette, keep only the skeleton, keep only the paths the joints trace. Each step removes something that could identify a person and keeps something that still might. Where identity actually disappears is not a property of the picture; it depends on what is stored, what it is combined with, how long it persists and what it is for.
Kind: Technical Article
Category: Privacy by Architecture
Topics: Responsible AI · Movement intelligence · Research
Published: 2026-09-30
Author: GaitAI Research
Reading time: 8 minutes
The question it answers: If the face is gone and only a skeleton remains, is anyone still identifiable?
Excerpt: RGB, face removed, silhouette, skeleton, joint trajectories: each representation removes some identifying cues and keeps others. Where identity disappears depends on storage, combination, persistence and purpose — not on the picture alone.
Opening: The most common privacy claim in movement AI is a diagram. A camera on the left, a stick figure on the right, an arrow between them, and the sentence "we only process skeletons". The diagram is honest about the engineering. It is not, on its own, a statement about privacy — and the field that made the engineering possible is the reason why. · Gait recognition is the study of identifying people by how they walk. Its best-known methods work from silhouettes and from skeletons: exactly the representations the diagram offers as the point where identity is gone. That is not a contradiction to be argued away. It is the fact a privacy architecture has to be built around. · The hero figure is illustrative — a drawn figure and a qualitative ledger, not a measurement of anyone's re-identifiability. The evidence links at the end point at the published surveys the argument draws on. Nothing here claims that any representation is anonymous.
What the reader takes away: The five kinds of identifying information a walking video carries · Why the gait-recognition literature is the strongest argument for privacy engineering · The six things privacy actually depends on — and representation is only one
The two-minute version: A walking video carries several kinds of identifying information at once: face, clothing and colour, body shape and proportions, the gait pattern itself, and the context of time and place. · Removing the face removes one of them. Clothing, build and gait are untouched; on their own they narrow a person down considerably. · A silhouette removes texture and colour but keeps shape and movement — the very signals a decade of gait-recognition research has learned to identify people from. · A skeleton removes appearance almost entirely, but pose sequences carry identity too; the research that makes GaitAI possible is the evidence. · Joint trajectories carry the least image information — and if they are stored with times and places, or matched across days, a pattern can still be re-identified. · Privacy depends on representation, storage, combination, persistence, purpose and deployment together. A diagram of the pipeline is not a privacy guarantee.
Sections: 01 What a walking video actually holds · 02 Removing the face is not anonymity · 03 Silhouettes and skeletons carry gait — and gait carries identity · 04 Trajectories, and the passage of time · 05 What privacy actually depends on · 06 Designing for honest privacy

docs.sectionTitle: What a walking video actually holds
docs.summary: It helps to name the kinds of identifying information a few seconds of video carries, because they are removed by different steps and they do not weigh the same. Five layers of identity in a walking video.
docs.content:
Article: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
Section: 01 What a walking video actually holds
It helps to name the kinds of identifying information a few seconds of video carries, because they are removed by different steps and they do not weigh the same.
Five layers of identity in a walking video. Illustrative grouping; the boundaries are not sharp. 01 Face: The strongest single cue, and the one most people think of as identity. 02 Appearance: Clothing, colour, hair, accessories. Weak alone; strong in combination, and stable across a day. 03 Shape: Height, build, limb proportions. Persistent across days and clothing. 04 Gait: The pattern of the walk itself — timing, rhythm, posture. The subject of an entire recognition literature. 05 Context: When and where. Two anonymous observations at the same door at the same time each morning are not anonymous for long.
Every stage of a privacy pipeline removes some of these and keeps others. The question is never "is identity gone" but "which layers remain, and what would it take to use them".

docs.sectionTitle: Removing the face is not anonymity
docs.summary: Blurring or masking the face is the first thing most systems do, and it should be: it removes the most recognisable region before anything is stored. It is also the step most often mistaken for the whole job. Look at what remains.
docs.content:
Article: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
Section: 02 Removing the face is not anonymity
Blurring or masking the face is the first thing most systems do, and it should be: it removes the most recognisable region before anything is stored. It is also the step most often mistaken for the whole job.
Look at what remains. The clothing is intact, and clothing is stable for a day. The build and proportions are intact, and they are stable for years. The walk is intact. In a small population — a ward, an office, a school — appearance and build alone narrow a person down to a handful, and the third Foundation's privacy figure showed exactly this: after face redaction the identity indicator barely moved.
A useful step, an incomplete claim: Face removal reduces the most direct route to identity and should be applied at the edge. Describing the result as anonymous is an overclaim, because four of the five layers are untouched.

docs.title: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
docs.sectionTitle: Silhouettes and skeletons carry gait — and gait carries identity
docs.summary: A silhouette discards texture and colour: no face, no clothing detail, no hair. What it keeps is the outline — shape and its movement over time. A skeleton discards even the outline, keeping a dozen joints and how they move.
docs.content:
Article: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
Section: 03 Silhouettes and skeletons carry gait — and gait carries identity
A silhouette discards texture and colour: no face, no clothing detail, no hair. What it keeps is the outline — shape and its movement over time. A skeleton discards even the outline, keeping a dozen joints and how they move.
This is where the diagram's argument is weakest, because these are the representations gait recognition was built on. Silhouette-based methods have identified people from outlines for two decades; model-based methods do it from skeletons and joint angles. The surveys in the evidence below collect hundreds of such results across clothing changes, carried objects and viewing angles. That research is what makes movement measurement possible at all — and it is also a demonstration that a skeleton is not an anonymised person.
What each representation removes and keeps. Qualitative; the strength of what remains depends on the population and the data around it. Removed — Gone by the skeleton stage: Face; Clothing, colour, hair; Most of the body's outline; Background and scene Kept — Still present in a skeleton: Limb proportions and height; The gait pattern — timing, rhythm, posture; Whatever context travels with the frames; A signature that recognition methods can learn
The skeleton is not where identity ends. It is where identity stops being visible to a person and starts being visible only to a model.

docs.title: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
docs.sectionTitle: Trajectories, and the passage of time
docs.summary: Reduce further and only movement remains: the paths a few joints trace, or the path a person takes through a room. This is the leanest representation a movement system can work from, and it is genuinely far from an image.
docs.content:
Article: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
Section: 04 Trajectories, and the passage of time
Reduce further and only movement remains: the paths a few joints trace, or the path a person takes through a room. This is the leanest representation a movement system can work from, and it is genuinely far from an image. A single trajectory, alone, identifies almost no one.
The word doing the work in that sentence is alone. Trajectories are recorded at a time, in a place. Keep them for a week and the same route at the same hour becomes a pattern. Join them to a door-access log, a rota, a room booking, and the pattern acquires a name. Match today's rhythm against yesterday's and a system that never stored a face is re-identifying a person by their walk — which is, once again, precisely the capability the recognition literature describes.
The privacy of a representation is not a property of the representation. It is a property of the representation together with how long it is kept, what it is stored next to and what it is compared against. A pipeline diagram shows none of those.

docs.title: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
docs.summary: Put the argument together and identity does not disappear at a stage; it is reduced by a set of decisions, each of which can be undone by another. Six of them decide the outcome. Representation.
docs.content:
Article: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
Section: 05 What privacy actually depends on
Put the argument together and identity does not disappear at a stage; it is reduced by a set of decisions, each of which can be undone by another. Six of them decide the outcome.
Representation. What survives the transformation: a skeleton keeps less than a silhouette, a trajectory less than a skeleton. Necessary, never sufficient. · Storage. Whether the reduced data is kept at all, for how long, and whether the original frames are kept alongside it. A skeleton next to its source video is a video. · Combination. What the data can be joined to: identity logs, timetables, other cameras, other sensors. Linkage is how anonymous data stops being anonymous. · Persistence. Whether observations of the same walk can be matched across days. A pattern that recurs is a signature. · Purpose. What the model is asked to do. A system built to count people in a corridor and a system built to recognise them can consume the same skeletons. · Deployment. Who operates it, who can query it, and what the people being observed have been told. Architecture sets the ceiling; governance decides where under it a system sits.
Representation is the one an engineering team controls most directly, which is why it is the one that gets drawn. The other five are where most real privacy failures happen.

docs.title: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
docs.summary: None of this argues against privacy engineering. It argues for doing all of it, and for describing it accurately. Minimise at the edge, and mean it. Transform before storage, not after.
docs.content:
Article: Can a Skeleton Still Reveal Identity?
Section: 06 Designing for honest privacy
None of this argues against privacy engineering. It argues for doing all of it, and for describing it accurately.
Minimise at the edge, and mean it. Transform before storage, not after. If the raw frames are never kept, four of the five layers never enter the system. · Do not keep what the purpose does not need. A counting system needs no trajectories from last week. Expiry is a privacy control. · Do not link by default. Movement data joined to identity data is identity data. Linkage should be a deliberate, disclosed decision. · Say what remains. "We process skeletons" is a description of the representation. "Skeletons can carry gait identity; here is what we do about that" is a description of the privacy. · Treat re-identification as a capability the system has, not one it lacks. The literature says it does. Govern accordingly.
The third Foundation called this privacy by architecture: sensing and identification as separable stages, separated on purpose. This story adds the caveat that keeps the phrase honest. The separation is not a place in the pipeline where identity is gone. It is a set of decisions that keep identity from being reassembled — and every one of them has to hold.

Can a skeleton still reveal identity? Yes — the research that makes movement intelligence possible is the proof. That is not an argument against skeleton-based systems; it is the reason their privacy has to be engineered in storage, linkage, persistence, purpose and governance, not declared by a diagram.

docs.title: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
docs.summary: A movement model can be right on every frame and the system built around it can still fail the person it was meant to help. Cameras drop frames, inference queues fill, networks stall, alerts arrive late or twice, dashboards hide the one that matters, and a tired operator dismisses the tenth false alarm of the shift. Model quality is one link in that chain. This is about the others.
docs.content:
Article: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
Subtitle: Everything between the camera and the person who acts
Standfirst: A movement model can be right on every frame and the system built around it can still fail the person it was meant to help. Cameras drop frames, inference queues fill, networks stall, alerts arrive late or twice, dashboards hide the one that matters, and a tired operator dismisses the tenth false alarm of the shift. Model quality is one link in that chain. This is about the others.
Kind: Engineering Note
Category: Engineering GaitAI
Topics: Engineering · Movement intelligence
Published: 2026-10-07
Author: GaitAI Research
Reading time: 8 minutes
The question it answers: If the model is right, why did the alert never arrive?
Excerpt: A model can be right on every frame while the system around it fails: dropped frames, stalled inference, a network that swallows an alert, an interface that hides it, a person who has stopped trusting it. Model quality is one link in the chain.
Opening: Most of the writing about movement AI, including a good deal of this journal, is about the model: what it sees, where it fails, what it should and should not claim. That is right, and it is not enough. A model does not help anyone. A system does — and the system is everything between the lens and the person who decides what to do. · This story follows that chain link by link. It is not a catalogue of things that go wrong for its own sake; it is an argument that reliability is a property of the whole, that most of the whole is not the model, and that a system has to be honest about its own state in exactly the way the earlier stories asked a model to be honest about its measurements. · The hero figure is a conceptual demonstration. It shows kinds of failure and their consequences as states, not as rates; no uptime, latency or accuracy figure appears anywhere in this article, and none should be inferred.
What the reader takes away: The six places a movement system fails that have nothing to do with the model · Why a late alert and a false alert are different engineering problems · What reliability means when the last component is a person
The two-minute version: A deployed movement system is a chain: capture, inference, transport, alerting, interface, human review. The model is one link. · Each link fails in its own way — a frozen camera, a saturated inference queue, a network partition, an alert that arrives twice or never, a dashboard that buries it, an operator who has learned to ignore it. · Most of these failures are invisible to the model. It keeps producing correct outputs for the frames it receives; the frames, or the outputs, simply stop going anywhere useful. · Late is a failure mode of its own. A correct alert that arrives after the moment it was for has the cost of a missed one and the cost of a false one. · Reliability has to be designed end to end: heartbeats, known-unknown states, idempotent alerts, honest interfaces, and a human workload the system does not exhaust. · The measure of a system is not the model's score. It is whether the right person saw the right thing in time — and knew when they could not.

docs.title: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
docs.summary: Camera → Inference → Network → Alert → Interface → Operator Six links between a movement and a decision. The model lives inside the second. Every deployed movement system has some version of this chain.
docs.content:
Article: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
Section: 01 The chain
Camera → Inference → Network → Alert → Interface → Operator Six links between a movement and a decision. The model lives inside the second.
Every deployed movement system has some version of this chain. A camera or sensor captures; a model, on a device or a server, infers; a network carries the result; an alerting layer decides what is worth someone's attention; an interface shows it; a person reads it and acts, or does not. The names vary, the order sometimes does, but the shape is constant.
The model's quality — everything the first Foundation and the AI Under Stress stories are about — decides how good the second link is. It says nothing about the other five. A system is only as reliable as the weakest of the six, and the weakest is rarely the one with the research literature behind it.
keywords: a good model can still be a bad system

docs.title: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
docs.sectionTitle: How each link fails, and what the model sees
docs.summary: The hero figure lets you break each link in turn. The right-hand column is the important one: what the model experiences while the system fails around it. In most cases, nothing. A failure per link, and the model's view of it.
docs.content:
Article: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
Section: 02 How each link fails, and what the model sees
The hero figure lets you break each link in turn. The right-hand column is the important one: what the model experiences while the system fails around it. In most cases, nothing.
A failure per link, and the model's view of it. Conceptual — kinds of failure, not frequencies. 01 Camera: A frozen frame, a smeared lens, a lost feed. The model receives fewer frames, or the same frame, and infers on what arrives. 02 Inference: A saturated queue, a throttled device, a stale model. Results arrive late or are skipped; the ones that arrive are correct. 03 Network: A partition, a retry storm, a buffer that fills and drops. Correct results leave the device and never arrive. 04 Alert: A threshold that fires twice, a deduplication that swallows a real event, a message queued behind a backlog. 05 Interface: The right alert on the wrong screen, in a colour that means nothing, below the fold of a list nobody scrolls. 06 Operator: The tenth alert of a shift dismissed without being read, because the first nine were wrong. The model was right about the tenth.
In five of the six failures, the model's outputs were correct. In all six, the person who needed them did not get them in time.

docs.title: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
docs.summary: Model evaluation asks whether an output is right. Systems have a second axis: when. A movement event — a fall, a stop, a change in gait that a clinician wanted to know about — has a window in which knowing about it is useful.
docs.content:
Article: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
Section: 03 Late is its own failure
Model evaluation asks whether an output is right. Systems have a second axis: when. A movement event — a fall, a stop, a change in gait that a clinician wanted to know about — has a window in which knowing about it is useful. An alert that arrives after the window is not a late success. It is a miss that also costs someone's attention.
Two alerts, one correct model. In time — The alert does its job: Arrives inside the window it was for; Costs one look; Builds trust when it is right Late — The alert costs twice: The event has already resolved, well or badly; Costs a look and a dismissal; Teaches the operator that alerts arrive after the fact
Latency accumulates along the chain: capture, inference, transport, queueing, rendering, noticing. Each stage adds a little; several add a lot under load, which is exactly when the events being watched for are most likely. A system that reports its own end-to-end delay, and knows when it has exceeded the window, is doing something the model cannot do for it.

docs.title: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
docs.sectionTitle: The system has to know when it does not know
docs.summary: The fifth Foundation drew a line between a missing input and a silently corrupted one: the first is a routing problem the system can see, the second a detection problem it may not. The same line runs through the whole chain.
docs.content:
Article: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
Section: 04 The system has to know when it does not know
The fifth Foundation drew a line between a missing input and a silently corrupted one: the first is a routing problem the system can see, the second a detection problem it may not. The same line runs through the whole chain. A camera that reports "no frames for thirty seconds" is a known unknown. A camera that keeps sending the same frozen frame is a silent one — and the model will infer a perfectly stationary person from it, correctly.
Heartbeats, not silence. Every link should say "I am here and this is my state" on a schedule, so that silence means failure rather than calm. · Staleness is a state. A result older than its window should be shown as stale, not as current. Age is data. · Duplicates are failures too. An alert delivered twice is not twice as safe; it is a sign the transport does not know what it delivered, and it costs attention. · Degraded is a mode. A system that has lost a camera should say so and keep running on what remains, rather than either stopping or pretending.
The stories before this one asked the model to withhold a measurement it could not support. This one asks the system to do the same about itself: to surface its own gaps as gaps, so that an absence of alerts is never mistaken for an absence of events.

docs.sectionTitle: The last link is a person
docs.summary: Everything upstream exists so that a person can decide something. That person is a component with its own failure modes, and they are not moral failings: attention is finite, trust is earned and lost by experience, and a screen full of…
docs.content:
Article: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
Section: 05 The last link is a person
Everything upstream exists so that a person can decide something. That person is a component with its own failure modes, and they are not moral failings: attention is finite, trust is earned and lost by experience, and a screen full of alerts that are usually wrong trains anyone to stop reading it. This is the oldest finding in alarm design, and movement AI is not exempt from it.
It follows that the number of alerts a system emits is a reliability decision, not just a sensitivity setting. A model tuned to miss nothing will, through the operator, end up missing a great deal. The decision support framing the Foundations insisted on is partly about this: the output is offered to a person to review, so the system has to be designed around what a person can actually review.
Design the workload, not just the model: How many alerts an hour; how they are ranked; what one look tells the operator; how a dismissal is recorded and learned from; what happens on the night shift. None of these is in the model's evaluation, and all of them decide whether the model's correctness reaches anyone.

docs.title: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
docs.summary: Reliability for a movement system is not the model's score and not the servers' uptime. It is a chain of properties, each of which has to hold: The capture is present and the system knows when it is not.
docs.content:
Article: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
Section: 06 What reliability means here
Reliability for a movement system is not the model's score and not the servers' uptime. It is a chain of properties, each of which has to hold:
The capture is present and the system knows when it is not. · The inference is current and the system knows when it is stale. · The transport delivers once and the system knows what it delivered. · The alert is in time and the system knows the window. · The interface shows the right thing first. · The person has a workload they can carry, and reasons to trust what they see.
A good model is the part of this that gets published. A good system is the part that gets deployed. GaitAI's own position is that the second is the product — and that it should be described, tested and reported as a chain, because that is what fails.

docs.content:
Article: A Good Model Can Still Be a Bad System
Section: Closing
A model that is right on every frame is necessary and not remotely sufficient. The frames have to arrive, the results have to travel, the alert has to land in time on a screen someone is looking at, and that someone has to have been given reason to believe it. Every one of those is engineering, and every one of them fails quietly.
Engineering GaitAI continues with the hardest version of this chain — the one that has to run in real time, where every link's latency is a link in its own right.

docs.title: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
docs.summary: Every movement measure needs something to be compared against. A population reference says where a person sits among strangers. A personal baseline — the same person, measured again and again under comparable conditions — says whether they have changed. The two can disagree about the same reading, and when they do, only one of them knows the person.
docs.content:
Article: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
Subtitle: The reference that makes a change readable
Standfirst: Every movement measure needs something to be compared against. A population reference says where a person sits among strangers. A personal baseline — the same person, measured again and again under comparable conditions — says whether they have changed. The two can disagree about the same reading, and when they do, only one of them knows the person.
Kind: Technical Article
Category: Inside the Signal
Topics: Mobility · Movement intelligence · Research
Published: 2026-10-14
Author: GaitAI Research
Reading time: 8 minutes
The question it answers: Why can a reading be normal for everyone and a change for this person?
Excerpt: A population reference says where a person sits among strangers; a personal baseline says whether they have changed. What a baseline is made of, how many observations it needs, when it moves, and what it can and cannot say.
Opening: Take any movement measure — cadence, symmetry, stride variability, a composite index — and ask what a single value of it means. On its own, nothing. It means something only next to a reference, and there are two very different references to choose from. · The fourth Foundation made the case that fall risk is a trend, not a number, and the symmetry story before this one ended on the same note: the informative reference is the person's own pattern. This story is about that reference itself. What a personal baseline is made of, how much of it you need, when it is allowed to move, and what it entitles a system to say. · The hero figure is illustrative: a drawn distribution and drawn observations, chosen to make the argument visible. There is no clinical threshold in this article and no value is stated as a number; the readings are phrases.
What the reader takes away: The difference between a threshold and a baseline, on one axis · What a baseline is actually made of — and why it has a width · When the baseline itself should be allowed to move
The two-minute version: A population reference is a distribution of strangers. It says whether a reading is unusual in general, and nothing about whether it is unusual for this person. · A personal baseline is the same person measured repeatedly under comparable conditions. It has a centre and a spread, because nobody walks identically twice. · A baseline needs enough observations to know its own spread. Three shows a tendency; more shows what ordinary variation looks like, which is what a change has to exceed. · Baselines move. Recovery, seasons, footwear and a new camera position all shift them; the system has to know whether the person or the setup changed. · Capture quality travels with the baseline. Observations made from different geometry are different instruments, and cannot be pooled without saying so. · A reading outside a personal baseline is context, not a finding. It is the reason for a closer look by someone qualified to take one.
Sections: 01 A threshold answers a different question · 02 What a baseline is made of · 03 How many observations is enough · 04 When the baseline itself should move · 05 Baselines and capture quality · 06 What a baseline can and cannot say
Reading-path position: Step 2 — The reference that knows the person

docs.title: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
docs.sectionTitle: A threshold answers a different question
docs.summary: A population reference is what most people picture when they hear "normal range": a distribution of many people's values, with a band across the middle that most of them fall inside.
docs.content:
Article: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
Section: 01 A threshold answers a different question
A population reference is what most people picture when they hear "normal range": a distribution of many people's values, with a band across the middle that most of them fall inside. Compare one reading against it and you learn where the person sits among strangers. That is a real question, and for some purposes the right one.
It is not the question most movement monitoring is asking. A care team, a physiotherapist, a coach or the person themselves usually wants to know whether something has changed — and a population band cannot say. Two people can sit at the same point in it for opposite reasons: one has always been there, one has drifted there from somewhere else. The reading is identical; the story is not.
The same reading, two references, two answers. Population — Where among strangers: Wide, because people differ; Says whether a value is unusual in general; Silent about direction of travel; Available from the first observation Personal — Whether this person changed: Narrow, because one person is consistent; Says whether a value is unusual for this person; Direction of travel is the reading; Needs several observations first
keywords: what is a personal movement baseline?
a threshold answers a different question

docs.title: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
docs.sectionTitle: What a baseline is made of
docs.summary: A personal baseline is not a value. It is a set of observations of the same measure, from the same person, made under conditions alike enough to compare — and it has two properties, both of which matter. A centre.
docs.content:
Article: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
Section: 02 What a baseline is made of
A personal baseline is not a value. It is a set of observations of the same measure, from the same person, made under conditions alike enough to compare — and it has two properties, both of which matter.
A centre. Where this person's readings tend to fall. Often nowhere near the population centre, and that is not a problem; it is the point. · A spread. How much the readings vary from one ordinary day to the next. Nobody walks identically twice, and the spread is what a change has to exceed before it counts as one.
The hero figure draws both. Bring the observations in one at a time and the first few form a cluster; the band drawn around them is the spread. The latest reading is then judged against that band — not against a number, and not against a population.
A baseline without a spread is a threshold with a personal name on it. The spread is what makes it a baseline.
keywords: what is a personal movement baseline?
what a baseline is made of

docs.title: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
docs.summary: There is no universal number, and any story that offers one should be read carefully. What a baseline needs is enough observations to know its own spread: to have seen what an ordinary good day and an ordinary bad day look like for this…
docs.content:
Article: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
Section: 03 How many observations is enough
There is no universal number, and any story that offers one should be read carefully. What a baseline needs is enough observations to know its own spread: to have seen what an ordinary good day and an ordinary bad day look like for this person, so that a reading outside that range means something.
Three observations show a tendency. More show the variation around it. The figure draws its band only once three are in and keeps widening it as ordinary variation appears — because a band drawn from two very consistent days would flag the third, perfectly ordinary, day as a change.
Consistency of capture matters more than the count. Five observations from the same corridor, the same camera and the same time of day form a better baseline than fifteen from wherever the person happened to be filmed. The next section is about why.
keywords: what is a personal movement baseline?

docs.title: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
docs.sectionTitle: When the baseline itself should move
docs.summary: A baseline describes a person at a period of their life, and people change. Someone recovering from an injury has a baseline that is supposed to move; freezing it at the first week would flag every improvement as an anomaly.
docs.content:
Article: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
Section: 04 When the baseline itself should move
A baseline describes a person at a period of their life, and people change. Someone recovering from an injury has a baseline that is supposed to move; freezing it at the first week would flag every improvement as an anomaly. Someone whose walk changes with the season, with new footwear or with a new routine has a baseline that has genuinely shifted, not a change worth a closer look.
Reasons a baseline moves, and what each asks of the system. Illustrative. 01 Recovery: The centre moves on purpose. The system should track the trajectory of the baseline, not alarm on it. 02 Season and routine: Slow drift with weather, footwear, activity. Expected; re-baselining on a schedule absorbs it. 03 A step change: A sudden, sustained shift. The reason a baseline exists — and the one case where the old baseline should be kept for comparison. 04 A change in setup: A moved camera, a new device, a different room. The baseline did not move; the instrument did. See the next section.
Telling these apart is not something the measure can do alone. It takes the history — how fast the centre moved and whether it stayed — and it takes a record of the conditions each observation was made under.

when the baseline itself should move

docs.title: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
docs.summary: The Engineering GaitAI story on camera angle made the point that two recordings from different mounts are two instruments. For a baseline this is decisive.
docs.content:
Article: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
Section: 05 Baselines and capture quality
The Engineering GaitAI story on camera angle made the point that two recordings from different mounts are two instruments. For a baseline this is decisive. If the observations that built the band came from a side-on camera and today's reading came from an oblique one, the reading is outside the band because the geometry changed — not because the person did.
Every observation carries its capture. Angle, distance, lighting, occlusion, which sensor. A baseline is built only from observations whose capture is comparable, or corrected to be. · A degraded capture does not enter the baseline. The fourth Foundation's figure showed an assessment with a degraded capture sitting in a sequence; it is shown, and it is not counted. · A change in setup resets the comparison, not the person. When the instrument changes, the honest reading is "not comparable yet", and the baseline starts again alongside the old one.
The baseline is a pair: A set of values and the conditions they were measured under. Store one without the other and the first surprising reading cannot be interpreted.
keywords: what is a personal movement baseline?

docs.title: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
docs.sectionTitle: What a baseline can and cannot say
docs.summary: A reading outside a personal baseline says one thing: this person's movement, measured this way, under these conditions, is not where it usually is.
docs.content:
Article: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
Section: 06 What a baseline can and cannot say
A reading outside a personal baseline says one thing: this person's movement, measured this way, under these conditions, is not where it usually is. That is a great deal more than a population threshold can say — and it is still not a finding.
It can say that something changed, in which measure, and roughly when. · It can say whether the change persists across observations or was one unusual day. · It cannot say why. Recovery, fatigue, footwear, a slope, a moved camera and a pose error all move a reading. · It cannot say what to do. It is offered to a person who can look at the history, the capture and the person — as decision support.
That is the whole design. The population reference answers a question about everyone. The personal baseline answers a question about someone — and it can only do that if it is built carefully, allowed to move for the right reasons, and kept together with the conditions that made it.
keywords: what is a personal movement baseline?
what a baseline can and cannot say

docs.title: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
docs.summary: A personal movement baseline is the reference that turns a measurement into context. It is made of repeated observations, it has a spread, it moves for reasons that have to be told apart, and it carries its capture with it.
docs.content:
Article: What Is a Personal Movement Baseline?
Section: Closing
A personal movement baseline is the reference that turns a measurement into context. It is made of repeated observations, it has a spread, it moves for reasons that have to be told apart, and it carries its capture with it. Built that way, it can say something a population threshold never could: not whether this reading is normal, but whether it is normal for you.

docs.title: How a GaitAI deployment starts
docs.summary: The five steps from defining an environment to running a pilot, and how pilot scope is set.
docs.content:
Deployment steps: Define the environment — Agree the setting and the question it has to answer — a clinic corridor, a ward, an academy, a concourse, a plant floor — and which outcome matters there. · Connect movement input — Point GaitAI at what already exists: a phone or clinic camera, existing CCTV or uploaded footage, or wearable and smartwatch signals. · Configure intelligence modules — Select the modules the environment needs. Products share one underlying movement-processing engine, so a single capture workflow can feed several of them. · Validate with the team — Clinicians or operators review real outputs against their own judgement, and zones, thresholds and report formats are tuned to the site. · Pilot and measure outcomes — Run the workflow in place, review what the movement record shows, and decide together what a wider rollout would need.
Pilot scope: Pilot scope and duration depend on the environment, integration requirements and the modules selected.

docs.title: How GaitAI works end to end
docs.summary: GaitAI works as a movement-intelligence pipeline: movement is captured from a video, camera or wearable signal, understood as pose and movement signals, measured as gait and movement features, interpreted by the relevant MobilityCare or SecureVision module, and returned as a report, dashboard or alert for a clinician or operator to review.
docs.content:
The pipeline in four steps (as the home page states it): 1. Capture Movement — A short walking video, CCTV feed, or smartwatch signal — captured wherever the person is, contactless. · 2. AI Understands Movement — Pose estimation, gait and activity feature extraction and sensor-fusion models translate motion into measurable signals. · 3. Insight, Report or Dashboard — Movement reports, mobility scores, operator dashboards or safety alerts are generated automatically. · 4. Clinician / Operator Acts — The right person — clinician, therapist, caregiver or security operator — receives the right signal, with the movement evidence behind it.
The five stages of the Try GaitAI walkthrough: 1. Capture — A few seconds of ordinary walking. No special camera, no markers, no lab. · 2. Pose — The body becomes positions, not pixels. Landmarks per frame. Appearance is not kept. · 3. Measure — One stride, segmented and read. Every reading is drawn from a specific part of the signal. · 4. Interpret — Features become movement intelligence. Compared against this person's own earlier walks. · 5. Act — A structured output somebody can act on. Reviewed by a clinician — never a diagnosis.
One movement signal, and what each reading of it looks for (the home page's "One movement. Many meanings."): Health — how well someone moves Walking speed, cadence, stride symmetry and joint motion — described for a clinician to read, not scored. · Recovery — how that changes over time The same measures repeated, so a session is read against that person's own earlier movement rather than a population threshold. · Identity — who is walking — governed use only A gait-consistency signal beside existing credentials, intended only for lawful, authorised deployments under human oversight. · Safety — what is happening in a space Movement events in a space — falls, restricted-zone entry, crowd flow — with identity not required by default. · Readiness — how movement holds up under load Movement change across a programme or under load, read against a personal baseline. Movement, never a fitness verdict.
Inputs GaitAI can start from: Walking video — A short clip from any standard camera · CCTV / fixed camera — An existing camera feed in the space · Wearable — Smartwatch or IMU signals · Mobile — Capture on a phone, review on mobile · Pose stream — Skeleton landmarks rather than pixels · Multiple sources — More than one of the above, together
MobilityCare pipeline, stage by stage (Movement Intelligence Lab): Video — A short walking clip, captured on request → Person / pose — Body landmarks per frame → Gait cycle — Frames segmented into strides → Movement features — Cadence, timing, symmetry, posture → Analytics — Compared against this person's own baseline → Report — A structured output for review
SecureVision pipeline, stage by stage (Movement Intelligence Lab): Video — An existing camera feed in the space → Movement extraction — People as movement, not identities → Trajectories — Paths through the space over time → Density / flow — Where it fills up, and which way it moves → Candidate events — Movement worth a second look → Operator view — What a trained reviewer sees
Movement signals the platform reads: Gait identity · Stride variability · Balance & postural sway · Cadence & rhythm · Step symmetry · Walking speed · Posture markers · Mobility decline · Rehabilitation progress · Fall-risk signals · Neurological movement signals · Trajectory & path · Behaviour patterns · Crowd movement
AI capabilities the modules are built on: Pose estimation · Gait analysis · Temporal modelling · Movement biometrics · Person re-identification · Human activity recognition · Trajectory analysis · Multimodal sensor fusion · Edge inference · Anomaly detection · Risk scoring · Privacy-aware analytics · Explainable reporting
One engine, two product families: Select the modules the environment needs. Products share one underlying movement-processing engine, so a single capture workflow can feed several of them. · MobilityCare (12 clinical, rehabilitation, sports, wearable and elderly-care modules) and SecureVision (12 privacy-aware security, safety and operations modules) are the product layer on the same movement-intelligence core.
Privacy and governance built into the pipeline: Non-identifying mode: The architecture is designed so skeleton-only processing can replace identifiable video as the analytic substrate, letting movement analytics run without identity. SecureVision is designed to lead with identity-free capabilities by default. · Processing location: Designed for edge and on-device inference as well as server-side processing; the optimised edge pipeline is the subject of the granted patent. Which mode a given site runs is a deployment decision. · Designed to support consent-based capture, encrypted transfer, configurable retention and role-based access, with activity logging and skeleton-only processing modes. Deployment requirements depend on the applicable environment, organization and jurisdiction.
Where a human decides: GaitAI outputs are decision support for a clinician, therapist, caregiver, researcher or security operator, who reviews the movement evidence behind them. MobilityCare outputs do not diagnose; SecureVision outputs are not autonomous enforcement.
What this describes: The published architecture and the illustrative Movement Intelligence Lab walkthrough — how the platform is designed to work, not a measured result or a validation claim.

docs.title: Privacy and security architecture
docs.summary: What the GaitAI architecture is designed to support, control area by control area — stated as capability, not as a running deployment.
docs.content:
Processing location: Designed for edge and on-device inference as well as server-side processing; the optimised edge pipeline is the subject of the granted patent. Which mode a given site runs is a deployment decision. (source: Patent 402202 · Edge inference capability)
Non-identifying mode: The architecture is designed so skeleton-only processing can replace identifiable video as the analytic substrate, letting movement analytics run without identity. SecureVision is designed to lead with identity-free capabilities by default. (source: PrivacyGuard · pipeline stages)
Face blur: Face blur is designed as an optional pipeline transformation stage that can be applied before analytics rather than after. (source: PrivacyGuard · processing pipeline)
Raw video handling: The pipeline is designed to transform raw streams into movement features, so analytics operate on those features rather than on raw footage. (source: PrivacyGuard · privacy stack)
Retention controls: Retention is intended to be configurable per data class, with schedules set per site, so clinical captures need be kept only as long as the care workflow requires. Actual periods are agreed per deployment. (source: PrivacyGuard · deployment · shared clinical privacy note)
Role-based access: An authorization layer is designed to mediate dashboard views so roles see only permitted data, with policy configured per site and per role. (source: PrivacyGuard · access model)
Audit logs: The design provides for logging of access and policy-change events, with audit logs exportable for an organisation's own compliance review. (source: PrivacyGuard · audit and policy logs)
Consent: Clinical assessments are intended to be captured with informed consent, with policy and consent records held alongside the audit log. (source: Shared clinical privacy note · PrivacyGuard output schema)
Data in transit: Captures are intended to be uploaded over encrypted channels. Transport and storage configuration is agreed per deployment. (source: Shared clinical privacy note)
Biometric and identity processing: Identity-bearing modules (ReID, AccessMotion, Watchlist) are gated behind stricter policy controls and are intended only for deployments with lawful authority, consent, access control and auditability. Where non-identifying movement intelligence is sufficient, that is the intended default. (source: Responsible-deployment policy · Watchlist product record)
Defence and other high-assurance uses: DefenceMotion is designed for governed, human-supervised defence applications involving personnel safety, readiness, rehabilitation and authorised facility operations. It is not designed for autonomous targeting or lethal decision-making. Readiness and rehabilitation modes run only for enrolled personnel with consent; access mode supplements existing credentials and never identifies or denies on its own. No defence deployment, customer or clearance is documented. (source: DefenceMotion product record · Responsible-deployment policy)
Training data: Privacy-preserving handling of gait datasets inside deep-learning pipelines is a published research area (IET Biometrics, 2022). (source: Publication: gait dataset privacy protection)
Scope of the controls: These are architectural capabilities of the GaitAI pipeline rather than a description of a running deployment; what a given site enables is agreed with it. Lawful basis, consent management and deployment decisions remain with the deploying organisation, and privacy-aware architecture is not a guarantee of anonymity. (source: PrivacyGuard · documented limitations)
EXPLICITLY NOT CLAIMED anywhere in the GaitAI record: SOC 2, ISO 27001 or any other security certification · HIPAA, GDPR or DPDP Act compliance certification · A specific guaranteed retention or deletion window · Guaranteed encryption of data at rest · Clinical approval, regulatory clearance or medical-device status · Measured accuracy, latency or performance figures · Replacement for clinician judgement or a standalone diagnosis · Proof of identity from a movement match alone · Guaranteed detection or prevention of safety incidents

hipaa, gdpr or dpdp act compliance certification

guaranteed encryption of data at rest

Blog subscription What is collected.
If you subscribe on the blog, an article page or in the footer, we store the email address you type, which of those three places you typed it, and the times the record was created and last changed.

Blog article views and likes Each journal article keeps a running count of views and likes in Google Firebase (Firestore).

If a like is registered, the same kind of marker is kept in local storage so the button reflects your own choice.

The products analyse how people move, which makes privacy an architectural decision rather than a policy footnote.
The pipeline is designed to work on movement features rather than identifiable video: skeleton-only processing, optional face blur applied before analytics, configurable retention, role-based access and logged activity are architectural capabilities, configured per deployment rather than guaranteed everywhere.

docs.title: Responsible AI
docs.summary: How GaitAI governs movement intelligence: identity-free capabilities by default, lawful authority for biometric and watchlist use, explainable outputs and no overclaiming.
docs.content:
Legal · Responsible AI Responsible AI commitment GaitAI reads human movement, which makes restraint part of the product rather than a caveat attached to it. SecureVision leads with anomaly detection, crowd flow, worker safety and post-event investigation — capabilities that do not require identification. Biometric, re-identification and watchlist capabilities are intended only for lawful, authorized deployments with appropriate governance, access control and auditability. PrivacyGuard, the privacy-preserving analytics layer, is designed to support skeleton-only analytics, optional face blur applied before analytics, role-based access, configurable retention and exportable audit logs, and GaitAI’s intended configuration is to have it on from the start of a SecureVision engagement. Which of those controls a given site actually enables is agreed with that site — this page describes architecture and intent, not the state of any running system. It is privacy-aware architecture — it minimises identifiable data and governs access — and not a guarantee of anonymity. Where the boundaries sit Decision support, not decisions. MobilityCare outputs are assessment and monitoring metrics; they do not diagnose medical conditions and do not replace clinical judgement. SecureVision surfaces movement events for a trained operator to review — it detects patterns, not intent. Explainable by construction. Every score is built from named movement features, so the person acting on it can see what moved the number. No overclaiming. GaitAI claims no compliance certification, clinical approval or measured accuracy figure.
